editorial.headline: Wholesale Clothing: Open Nationally, Blocked for PMA Registration in Bali
editorial.standfirst: Wholesale clothing and apparel accessories are nationally open to PMA at every listed scale, but Bali blocks PMA registration under its permanent risk-based moratorium.
editorial.body:
At its core, this is the wholesale trade in clothing: garments moving through trade channels, including sportswear. The stated scope also includes clothing accessories—gloves, ties, clips and socks. That detail matters. The activity is not confined to garments alone; it embraces the named accessories alongside them. Sportswear sits within the garment coverage, while the accessories are expressly itemised rather than left to implication. Its practical centre is therefore clear and specific: the wholesale distribution of clothing and those accessories.

The registration picture is broad on scale. The activity is open to Mikro, Kecil, Menengah and Besar businesses, so the record places it across every listed size category rather than reserving it for a single tier. All four labels are stated in the record, providing the complete scale view it supplies. At national level, its PMA status is TERBUKA and its foreign-ownership ceiling is 100%. In straightforward terms, the national record permits foreign ownership up to 100% for this activity. That national position is significant, but it is only one part of the location question.

In Bali, the outcome changes. The provincial status is BLOCCATO_CLASSE_RISCHIO, and PMA registration is blocked. The stated reason is that, at the Besar scale, every scope has a Rendah or Menengah-Rendah—Low or Medium-Low—OSS risk classification; that brings the activity within Bali’s moratorium of May 13, 2026. The moratorium applies island-wide and on a permanent basis, according to the rule supplied with this record. Nationally, the foreign-ownership ceiling is 100%, but a foreign investor cannot register this activity in Bali today. The apparent contradiction is resolved by reading the national ownership setting and the Bali registration rule as separate facts.

Bali’s rule is not a lower local foreign-ownership percentage for this activity. It is a bar on PMA registration under the relevant risk treatment recorded here. The national ceiling remains 100%; it does not override the Bali outcome. A national ownership permission speaks to the permissible stake, while the Bali bar answers whether PMA registration can proceed in that location. For a founder deciding where to establish this activity, the honest conclusion is exact rather than conditional: the activity is nationally open to PMA across the listed scales, yet Bali does not allow its PMA registration under this moratorium.
